evidence.name: The Beresford
evidence.address: 211 Central Park West (aka 1-9 West 81st Street; 2-12 West 82nd Street)

claims.text: The Beresford is a cooperative apartment building at 211 Central Park West, between 81st and 82nd Streets, on the Upper West Side of Manhattan in New York City, United States.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1370202541 (edited 2026-08-19). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: It was constructed in 1929 and was designed by architect Emery Roth.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1370202541 (edited 2026-08-19). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: The Beresford is 22 stories tall and is topped by octagonal towers on its northeast, southwest, and southeast corners.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1370202541 (edited 2026-08-19). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: The building is a contributing property to the Central Park West Historic District, a National Register of Historic Places–listed district, and is a New York City designated landmark.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1370202541 (edited 2026-08-19). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: By the late 1920s, high-rise apartment buildings were being developed on Central Park West in anticipation of the completion of the New York City Subway's Eighth Avenue Line, which opened in 1932.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1370202541 (edited 2026-08-19). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: Central Park West was concurrently widened from 48 to 63 feet (15 to 19 m).
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1370202541 (edited 2026-08-19). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: Under the Multiple Dwelling Act of 1929, this allowed the construction of proportionally taller buildings on the avenue.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1370202541 (edited 2026-08-19). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: The Beresford, with its three relatively short towers, had been designed just before the passage of the act.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1370202541 (edited 2026-08-19). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: It contrasted with the multi-story twin towers of the Century, the Majestic, the San Remo, and the El Dorado, which were all built one to two years after the Beresford was completed.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1370202541 (edited 2026-08-19). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: As Christopher Gray of The New York Times wrote: "Had the Beresford been designed a year later, its three towers would have sprouted up like Jack's beanstalk."
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1370202541 (edited 2026-08-19). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: The Beresford Central Park West Corporation, headed by Bennett Gordon, acquired the old Hotel Beresford from Frederick Brown in March 1925.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1370202541 (edited 2026-08-19). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: Sugarman and Berger filed plans the next year for a high-rise apartment building to replace the hotel.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1370202541 (edited 2026-08-19). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: The LPC building database lists 211 Central Park West (aka 1-9 West 81st Street; 2-12 West 82nd Street) (The Beresford): architect/builder Emery Roth; primary style neo-Renaissance; date 1928 - 1929; historic district Upper West Side / Central Park West Historic District.
claims.uncertainty: Transcribed from the LPC Individual Landmark and Historic District Building Database. Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

evidence.name: The El Dorado
evidence.address: 300 Central Park West (aka 1-13 West 90th Street, 2-20 West 91st Street)

claims.text: The El Dorado (also spelled the Eldorado) is a cooperative apartment building at 300 Central Park West, between 90th and 91st Streets adjacent to Central Park, on the Upper West Side of Manhattan in New York City, United States.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1373447224 (edited 2026-09-06). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: It was constructed from 1929 to 1931 and was designed by architect of record Margon & Holder and consulting architect Emery Roth in the Art Deco style.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1373447224 (edited 2026-09-06). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: The El Dorado consists of twin 12-story towers rising from a 17-story base.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1373447224 (edited 2026-09-06). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: The building is a contributing property to the Central Park West Historic District, a National Register of Historic Places–listed district, and is a New York City designated landmark.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1373447224 (edited 2026-09-06). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: By the late 1920s, high-rise apartment buildings were being developed on Central Park West in anticipation of the completion of the New York City Subway's Eighth Avenue Line, which opened in 1932.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1373447224 (edited 2026-09-06). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: Central Park West was concurrently widened from 48 to 63 ft (15 to 19 m).
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1373447224 (edited 2026-09-06). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: Under the Multiple Dwelling Act of 1929, this allowed the construction of proportionally taller buildings on the avenue.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1373447224 (edited 2026-09-06). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: In March 1929, developer Frederick Brown acquired the original El Dorado Apartments, as well as eight adjacent row houses on 90th and 91st Streets.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1373447224 (edited 2026-09-06). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: The assemblage measured 200 ft (61 m) long on Central Park West and 90th Street and 175 ft (53 m) long on 91st Street.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted from Wikipedia revision 1373447224 (edited 2026-09-06). Claims are quoted or transcribed from the cited source; they are not independently verified.

claims.text: Three weeks later, Brown resold the sites to Louis Klosk, a Bronx-based developer who planned to erect a similarly named 22-story apartment building at a cost of $8.5 million.

claims.text: Early plans called for a 16-story building with a streamlined base and a flat top.
